title: Why Specimen Transport Timing Can Change a Diagnosis
excerpt: The 2-hour window between collection and lab analysis isn't arbitrary — it's the difference between a reliable result and a repeat test. Here's what Edmonton clinics need to know.
body:
When a patient's blood draw sits in a waiting room for three hours before heading to DynaLIFE, the results that come back may not reflect what was actually happening in their body at the time of collection. Potassium levels rise as red blood cells break down. Glucose decreases. Certain enzymes degrade. The 2-hour threshold for most specimen types isn't arbitrary — it's built on decades of laboratory medicine research.

What Happens After Collection

The moment blood enters a collection tube, a countdown begins. Most routine chemistry panels remain stable for 4–6 hours if properly refrigerated, but transportation to an unrefrigerated courier vehicle followed by stops at multiple pickup points can compress that window significantly. For glucose testing, every additional 30 minutes at room temperature can drop the reading by 5–7%. For coagulation studies, delay can dramatically affect PT/INR accuracy.

The Practical Impact for Edmonton Clinics

Edmonton has an unusual geography for specimen logistics. Clinics in the south (Windermere, Heritage Valley) face longer transport times to the DynaLIFE processing centre in the University area than downtown practices. A general courier running a mixed route of documents and medical specimens may not prioritize the temperature-sensitive cargo — and rarely tracks transit time.

What a Dedicated Medical Courier Does Differently

A healthcare-specific courier service like Speedo Medical treats every specimen pickup as time-sensitive. Routes are planned around collection windows, not package volume. Insulated carriers maintain sample integrity. And the dispatcher knows the difference between a STAT troponin for a suspected MI and a routine lipid panel — because dispatch priority matters.

If your clinic is using a general courier for lab runs, ask them: what's the average transit time from pickup to drop-off at the lab? If they can't answer that question, your patients' results may be arriving with a silent asterisk attached.

title: Cold-Chain Vaccine Delivery: What Edmonton Pharmacies Must Know
excerpt: A single temperature excursion can render an entire lot of vaccines unusable. Learn how purpose-built cold-chain courier protocols protect your inventory — and your patients.
body:
When Pfizer or Moderna vaccines arrive at a pharmacy, they come with strict temperature requirements: 2–8°C for most inactivated vaccines, -15 to -25°C for some mRNA products. What happens after they leave the wholesaler matters just as much as what happened during long-haul transport. The 'last mile' — the delivery from distributor to pharmacy, or pharmacy to long-term care facility — is where many cold-chain failures actually occur.

Alberta Health Services Cold Chain Requirements

AHS requires that all publicly-funded immunizing agents be maintained within defined temperature ranges at every point in the supply chain. Pharmacies are responsible for documenting cold-chain integrity from the moment they receive product. A courier without proper insulated carriers, temperature logs, or monitoring is an unacceptable link in that chain — not just for compliance reasons, but for patient safety.

What 'Medically Rated' Actually Means

A styrofoam cooler with a gel pack from a grocery store is not a medical-grade cold chain solution, even if the temperature happens to stay within range. Medical couriers use validated insulated carriers with calibrated phase-change materials that maintain precise temperature ranges regardless of ambient conditions — critical in Edmonton winters where an uninsulated vehicle cabin can drop below -30°C, and summers where vehicle interiors can exceed 40°C.

The Pharmacy-to-LTC Delivery Gap

One of the highest-risk cold-chain transfer points in Edmonton isn't the wholesaler. It's the routine delivery from a pharmacy to a long-term care facility. A driver who runs five LTC facilities in a route needs to maintain temperature throughout multi-stop delivery — not just at origin and destination. This requires equipment, training, and documentation that general couriers simply aren't designed to provide.

title: How Edmonton LTC Facilities Are Streamlining Medication Delivery
excerpt: Medication errors in long-term care cost lives and liability. Discover how dedicated courier routing is changing the way Edmonton nursing homes receive blister packs and unit-dose medications.
body:
A nursing home in south Edmonton has 120 residents. Each receives an average of 8 medications per day. Those medications arrive weekly from the dispensing pharmacy in blister packs, organized by resident and time of day. One missed delivery — or one delivery to the wrong facility — creates a cascade of phone calls, emergency prescriptions, and staff overtime that the care team can't afford. And more importantly, residents may miss critical doses.

The Problem with Ad-Hoc Delivery

Many Edmonton pharmacies that serve LTC facilities use whoever is available for delivery — sometimes a general courier, sometimes a pharmacy staff member, sometimes a contracted driver who also delivers for restaurants. None of these options offer the consistency, accountability, or medication-handling training that LTC environments require. When a blister pack goes missing, determining whether it was delivered, signed for, or left at the wrong door can take hours.

What a Dedicated LTC Route Looks Like

A purpose-built LTC delivery route assigns the same courier to the same facilities at the same time each day. The charge nurse knows who to expect. The courier knows which resident wing receives which pharmacy's deliveries. Electronic delivery confirmation means the pharmacy and the facility both have a timestamped record. Exceptions — a refused delivery, a signature discrepancy — are escalated immediately rather than discovered at the next business day's review.

The Accountability Gap

Under Alberta's continuing care standards, LTC operators are responsible for ensuring medication reaches residents. When a delivery goes wrong, the question of who is responsible can fall into a grey zone between the pharmacy, the courier, and the facility. Clear delivery documentation, chain of custody from pharmacy to care staff, and photo confirmation eliminate that ambiguity — and protect all parties.

title: STAT Medical Courier vs. General Courier: The Difference in an Emergency
excerpt: When a referring physician calls for an urgent specimen or time-critical medication, 'we'll get it there by end of day' is not an acceptable answer. Here's why STAT courier capability matters.
body:
STAT in medical parlance means immediately. It doesn't mean 'as soon as our next driver is available' or 'within our standard 4-hour window.' For most general couriers, STAT is a fee category, not an operational state. They'll charge an upcharge for urgency, but dispatch still goes through the same queue, the same route planning, the same driver who's halfway across the city on another run.

What True STAT Dispatch Requires

A real STAT medical courier service maintains capacity for immediate dispatch. That means not scheduling every driver at 100% utilization, so that when a call comes in at 2:17 PM for an urgent troponin that needs to reach the cardiac unit at the Grey Nuns, a driver is available to move in under 10 minutes. It means the dispatcher recognizes a STAT request as a priority over everything else in queue. And it means communication: the receiving facility knows exactly when the driver left origin and when they'll arrive.

The Time-Sensitivity of Common STAT Requests

Not all urgent requests are life-or-death emergencies, but many have hard clinical time windows. Blood cultures need to reach the lab before temperature changes invalidate results. Oral chemotherapy for outpatient treatment needs to reach a patient's home before their scheduled administration time. A coagulation control specimen before a procedure can't wait while the driver completes a scheduled pharmaceutical delivery in another part of the city.

Building STAT Capability Into Your Supply Chain

For clinics and pharmacies in Edmonton, establishing a relationship with a STAT-capable medical courier before you need one is essential. Waiting until you have a STAT need and then calling a number you've never tested is how urgent deliveries become near-misses. A dedicated medical courier like Speedo Medical builds STAT capability into every account — so when the call comes in, the answer is already 'yes.'

title: Medical Courier Coverage in Edmonton: Who Can Actually Reach Your Patients?
excerpt: Not all medical couriers serve the same areas. We break down Edmonton's delivery geography and explain why coverage breadth matters for pharmacies, labs, and hospitals.
body:
Edmonton is a sprawling city. The distance from the Henday loop in the northeast to the communities of Heritage Valley in the south is over 45 kilometres. A pharmacy in Windermere and a patient in Fort Saskatchewan are both 'Edmonton area' but separated by an hour's drive. When a courier service says they cover Edmonton, it's worth asking exactly what that means.

The Gap Between 'Edmonton' and Edmonton

Many courier services operate primarily in the downtown core and the major commercial corridors. They cover the hospitals near the University, the clinics in Oliver, the labs in the medical district. But the southwest communities, the rural Strathcona County addresses, the Leduc-area patients — these are often served by exception rather than by design, or not at all.

Why Coverage Geography Matters for Healthcare

A pharmacy that fills prescriptions for patients across all of Edmonton needs a courier that can reach all of Edmonton. If your courier can't deliver to Sherwood Park or St. Albert, you're either turning down patients or managing two courier relationships, which doubles coordination overhead and creates accountability gaps when something goes wrong at the handoff.

Speedo Medical's Edmonton Coverage

Speedo Medical serves the complete Edmonton metro area — from the core to the surrounding communities including St. Albert, Sherwood Park, Leduc, Beaumont, Fort Saskatchewan, and Spruce Grove. Our route planning accounts for Edmonton's traffic patterns, construction seasonality, and the geographic distribution of healthcare facilities. When we say we serve Edmonton, we mean the Edmonton your patients actually live in.

title: Choosing the Right Delivery Partner for Your Edmonton Pharmacy
excerpt: A courier change affects your patients, your staff, and your liability exposure. Here are the six questions every pharmacy owner should ask before signing a delivery contract.
body:
A pharmacy's delivery operation is an extension of its clinical service. The courier who drops off a patient's blood pressure medication is the last touchpoint in a chain that began with a physician visit, a diagnosis, and a prescription. Getting that last link right matters — both for patient outcomes and for your pharmacy's reputation.

Question 1: Are They Healthcare-Specific?

A courier that also delivers restaurant food, office supplies, and parcels isn't wrong — but they aren't optimized for healthcare. Their drivers may not know the handling protocols for controlled substances, biologics, or refrigerated medication. Their dispatch system prioritizes volume over timing sensitivity. Ask your prospective courier: what percentage of your volume is healthcare?

Question 2: What's Their Chain of Custody Process?

If a patient calls to say they never received their medication, can your courier tell you who signed for it, when, and where? Photo confirmation at delivery is a minimum standard. Electronic proof of delivery that syncs to your pharmacy management system is better. A driver who scribbles in a paper log is not good enough for a controlled substance delivery.

Question 3: How Do They Handle Cold-Chain Items?

Ask specifically about their equipment — not their policy, their equipment. What insulated carriers do they use? Do they use phase-change materials or ice packs? How do they handle deliveries on a -25°C January morning in Edmonton?

Question 4: What Is Their Response Time for STAT Requests?

Not average delivery time — STAT response. When a patient calls at 4:30 PM because they forgot to refill and are out of insulin, how long until a driver is dispatched? Get a number and test it.

Question 5: Do They Have Liability Coverage?

Courier companies should carry cargo insurance and general liability. For a pharmacy, you want to understand how loss or damage claims work for prescription medications — which have regulatory requirements around disposal and replacement that general cargo claims don't address.

Question 6: Who Do You Call When Something Goes Wrong?

Ask for the after-hours escalation number, not the main line. If your courier can only take complaints during business hours, you'll find out what that means when your most urgent delivery goes wrong on a Saturday afternoon.
